title: The abbot (ch. 2)
hook: the abbot holds the place of Christ and must adapt to each person

segments.voice: Yesterday, a school for beginners: Benedict hoped to set down nothing harsh or heavy. Your line was nothing harsh.

Should a good boss treat everyone the same? It sounds like fairness: same rules, same tone, same speech for the whole team. But a coach who barks at every player the same way loses some of them. One needs a push. One needs a joke. One needs to be left alone until Thursday. Saint Benedict's Rule has a chapter on the person in charge of the monastery, and it asks something harder than sameness.
screen: `TREAT EVERYONE THE SAME?` → `ONE NEEDS A PUSH, ONE A JOKE.` → `THE PERSON IN CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Chapter two starts high. The abbot is believed to hold the place of Christ in the monastery, because he's called by Christ's own name for the Father: abba. Benedict points to Paul, who says in the Douay-Rheims that we have received a spirit "whereby we cry: Abba (Father)." So abbot, in the Rule's own words, is a father's name. Then the chapter turns the weight around. Because he holds that place, the abbot will answer to God for every soul in his care. He's to teach more by what he does than by what he says. He's not to put a monk born free ahead of one who came from slavery. And he has to fit himself to each person: their character, their understanding. Coax one. Correct another. Reason with a third. Some respond to a gentle word; others need it said plainly. He should serve many temperaments, the Rule says, so that none of the flock is lost. Notice what Benedict isn't saying. The rules don't change for favorites. The same care wears different clothes for different people. Every monk gets the abbot's full attention, not the same speech. The Rule knows it's hard, calling the role difficult and demanding work: ruling souls. A father's name, a heavy account, and a habit of looking at each face before speaking.
screen: `A FATHER'S NAME: ABBA.` · `HE ANSWERS FOR EVERY SOUL.` · `COAX, CORRECT, REASON.` · `SAME CARE, DIFFERENT CLOTHES.` · then, large: `WHEREBY WE CRY: ABBA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people you look after, work with or live with, and picture them side by side. Ask what each needs from you right now: maybe one needs a push and the other gentleness, one more words and the other fewer, and just let their two faces be different. If you pray, ask God for the wisdom to care for each of them as they are.
Abbot. The father of a monastery, named, the Rule says, from abba, who holds the place of Christ and must fit himself to each person in his care. Today's word.
Your line: each one differently. Every face gets full attention, if not the same words. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Benedictine monasteries the monks elect their abbot or abbess, who leads the community and is responsible for each member's care, following chapter 2 of the Rule.

chat.says: Does a good abbot treat every monk exactly the same way?
options: Same care for all, but he fits himself to each: coaxing one, correcting another.
Yes. The Rule says one speech for everyone, so nobody can ever claim favorites.
No. He gives the senior and free-born monks more attention than all the rest.
chat.meaning: The Rule asks the abbot to adapt to each monk's character so none is lost, and never to favor the free-born over the formerly enslaved.

abba.meaning: father; the name the abbot's title comes from

ruling souls.meaning: the Rule's phrase for the abbot's hard work of care

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old Catholic English translation of the Bible

notes: Chapter 2 is paraphrased (Gasquet 1909 wording unverified). Points to confirm: 'Christi enim agere vices in monasterio creditur' with the appeal to Romans 8:15; teaching more by deeds than words; no favoritism for birth or wealth; adapting to 'multorum servire moribus'; 'rem difficilem et arduam, regere animas'; giving account for every soul.
The abbot/abba link is given as the Rule's own words, not as an independent etymology.
Greek of Romans 8:15 has 'Αββα ὁ πατήρ'; the original game shows ἀββα (breathing mark, no accent); editions vary (Αββα, ἀββά). Keeper to confirm.
howItsDone mentions abbesses and election (ch. 64); confirm.
